newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Planemaker Fokker set to close - receivers.
newsitem.headline: Planemaker Fokker set to close - receivers.

text.p: (Adds background, DASA comment, previous Amsterdam)

Planemaker Fokker has virtually no chance of staying in business after a key supplier pulled out, leading to the collapse of rescue talks with Korean conglomerate Samsung, the administrators said Thursday.

Fokker, one of the world's oldest aviation firms, has been hit by big losses as aircraft markets have stagnated. Industry observers say it could be heading for an undignified ending -- a piecemeal sale of its remaining assets to the highest bidder.

Administrators said they broke off negotiations with Samsung Aerospace after Belfast, Ireland-based aerospace firm Short Brothers Plc had said it would no longer supply wings for Fokker aircraft. Shorts is part of Bombardier Incof Canada.
"Administrators are therefore forced to conclude that a re-launch of Fokker of the basis of continuing current production is no longer feasible," they said in a statement.
They said there was very little chance of an alternative rescue plan going ahead with another wing supplier.
"The chances that the Fokker (aircraft) programme could survive on the basis of such a plan are minimal," they said in a statement.

Administrators who have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March gave Samsung of South Korea the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books in September with a view to a possible bid for its core plane-making business.
"It goes without saying that Fokker...will continue to make aircraft already ordered by KLM Cityhopper, Vietnam Airlines and Ethiopian Airlines," they said.
The administrators said that Samsung had informed them earlier Thursday that they would need another month to decide on whether to take over Fokker.
They said they had tried to extend the supply agreement with supplier firms, but Shorts had said it was no longer prepared to provide wings for Fokker's F-70 and F-100 jets.
In July, industrial services group Stork NV bought Fokker's profitable aircraft maintenance activities.
Most of the companies who showed an interest in Fokker in the early days of the bankruptcy, such as Shorts' parent Bombardier, have long since disappeared from the scene.
Russia's Yakovlev says it remains interested, but is not regarded in the Netherlands as a serious partner for Fokker.
Many of the other players in the overcrowded and fiercely competitive regional jet market would probably be glad to see the administrators bang the last nail into Fokker's coffin.

Fokker, founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, is one of the oldest names in the industry and its F27 Friendship turboprop, launched in 1957, was one of the industry's biggest commercial successes.
But in more recent years Fokker struggled to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.
In 1993 Daimler Benz Aerospace (DASA) paid 686 million guilders ($405 million) for a 51 percent stake in Fokker.

But despite job cuts and tight cost control, depressed world aircraft markets and a weak dollar saw the company steadily lose altitude and sink into deeper and deeper losses which had to be met by DASA and the Dutch government.
DASA said Thursday it hoped that Fokker could still be saved but it was prepared for it to be wound up.
In January 1996, Daimler said it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses and cut off all financial support, forcing the company into bankruptcy two months later.
